Its nonreduced fibre prevents étaleness, in agreement with the criterion requiring étale fibres (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 03PC](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03PC), Proposition 59.26.2). This is a counterexample to the isolated residue-field-only wording as transcribed, not to the stronger condition printed immediately afterward or to an unseen theorem elsewhere.

The manuscript says the ordinary-direct-image analogue would force a vanishing off an open set “ce qui n'est pas vrai si $f$ non propre.” An explicit model is $j:\mathbb G_{m,k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k$, with $k$ algebraically closed, $L=\Lambda$ on $\mathbb G_m$ and $M=j_!\Lambda$ for a finite field of coefficients: at a geometric point over $0$, $(Rj_*L)\otimes^{\mathbf L}M$ has zero stalk, whereas $Rj_*(L\otimes j^*M)$ has nonzero $H^0$ stalk. This adds a concrete boundary calculation to the manuscript's mechanism; the connected punctured strict-local neighbourhood gives the nonzero constant section.
**Confidence:** high — the two stalks differ already in degree zero.

The manuscript uses one fixed interval for “tout pt géom,” a quantifier that should be retained in any reconstruction. On a disjoint union of infinitely many points, put a copy of $A$ in cohomological degree $-n$ on the $n$th component: this is locally perfect and bounded above, with finite Tor-amplitude at every stalk, but it has no single global finite amplitude interval. The example distinguishes the manuscript's uniform claim from the local perfectness criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 08G8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08G8)); it does not refute the fixed-interval stalkwise criterion on the page.

The principal handwritten sequence concerns derived operations, projection and Künneth, traces over finite coefficient rings, Tor bounds and the beginning of a Lefschetz–Verdier construction. It supports the README's broad SGA 4/5 placement, while the **24 reused typescript pages** also contain operator theory, ramification, relative divisors, local algebra and an axiomatic étale-topos exposition. Those typed sources are not silently assigned to Grothendieck's authorship or treated as his own conjectures.

The assertion that the normalization of a one-dimensional local domain is a semilocal PID is correct under the usual Noetherian convention: normalization is semilocal Dedekind, and its invertible ideals are principal (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tags 09IG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09IG), [09N2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09N2), [02M9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02M9)). Thus absence of module-finite normalization or excellence is not by itself a gap in this lemma. What remains to recover is the reused source's convention for “local domain,” which is not spelled out in the surviving statement; a non-Noetherian reading would be a materially different claim.

The typed parenthesis “then $R=k[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]$” is not a consequence of equal characteristic and a regular system of parameters alone: $R=\mathbb Q[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ is countable and has coefficient field $\mathbb Q$, whereas $\mathbb Q[[x,y]]$ is uncountable. The primary complete-local theorem explicitly assumes completeness (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 0C0S](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0C0S)). This is a conditional counterexample to the isolated wording, and the right next step is to recover earlier conventions from the reused source before declaring its full theorem false.
